---
title: "Mixtures: Choose a Generator"
---

Two machines can produce the same kinds of values. Before each observation, a selector chooses which machine to use.

The output has one source at a time. Its probability law must account for that choice.

## 🔰 Put the selector into the experiment {#sec-sample-mixtures-put-the-selector-into-the-experiment}

Suppose machine A always emits zero and machine B always emits one.

Choose A with probability $0.75$ and B with probability $0.25$. The output is then zero with probability $0.75$ and one with probability $0.25$.

The selector has turned two deterministic sources into a random output.

More generally, let the source laws be $p_A[f]$ and $p_B[f]$. If the selector chooses A with probability $\alpha$ and B with probability $1-\alpha$, then

$$
p_{\mathrm{mix}}[f]
=
\alpha p_A[f]+(1-\alpha)p_B[f].
$$

This assumes each selected source follows its stated conditional law. The mixture weights record the selection probabilities.

## 🏵 The source label explains the addition {#sec-sample-mixtures-the-source-label-explains-the-addition}

The event “output is $f$” can occur by two disjoint routes:

- Select A and let A emit $f$.
- Select B and let B emit $f$.

We add the probabilities of those routes. The source label is part of the hidden joint description even when the final record omits it.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sample-mixture
%%| fig-cap: "The selector chooses one source for an output. Both routes can produce the same recorded value."
flowchart TD
    C["Source selector"] -->|"Weight alpha"| A["Generator A"]
    C -->|"Weight 1 minus alpha"| B["Generator B"]
    A --> Y["One recorded output"]
    B --> Y
```

## ⚙️ Mixing and adding answer different questions {#sec-sample-mixtures-mixing-and-adding-answer-different-questions}

If A always emits zero and B always emits one:

- Choosing one source produces either zero or one.
- Generating from both and adding produces one every time.

The same two source descriptions support two different experiments.

For probability vectors, a convex combination such as $\alpha p_A+(1-\alpha)p_B$ describes source selection. It does not describe addition of their numerical outcomes.

## 💡 Decide how often the selector is used {#sec-sample-mixtures-decide-how-often-the-selector-is-used}

A fresh, independent source choice for every observation can produce a sequence of independent mixture draws, if the component generators also supply the required fresh independent draws.

Choosing the source once for an entire run creates a different relationship. In our deterministic example, every run is then all zeros or all ones.

The one-observation mixture law is the same in either case. Their sequence laws differ because the selector's state persists in only one of them.

This returns us to the central question of [Generators](generators.qmd): what is remembered between outputs?

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-mixtures-try-the-idea}

A fair selector chooses between a fair six-sided die and a machine that always emits six. What is the probability of observing six? Does the output ever exceed six?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-mixtures-work-it-through}

The probability is $(1/2)(1/6)+(1/2)(1)=7/12$. No output exceeds six because the experiment chooses one source; it does not add their outputs.
:::
